clue.text: In commentary, appreciated extent of bridging needed for pot

indicators.note: a commentary is spoken, so the words are to be heard rather than read

parts.note: appreciated means saw, as in understood; the extent a bridge covers is its span

explanation.surface: A sports or radio commentator remarks on how far some bridge reached, oddly linked to a pot.
explanation.walkthrough: SAW SPAN, said quickly, sounds like the kitchen item.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is a cooking pot with a handle, so pot names it by a broader term.

clue.text: Piece of publicity about Long Kesh caused astonishment

indicators.note: the advertisement goes round, so the prison name sits inside it

parts.note: an advertisement, shortened to AD
Long Kesh was the Northern Ireland prison also known as the Maze

explanation.surface: A publicity piece about the notorious prison stirred up shock.
explanation.walkthrough: Long Kesh, the Northern Ireland internment prison, was later renamed HMP Maze.
explanation.definitionFit: To amaze is to astonish greatly, so the past-tense verb matches caused astonishment.

clue.text: Conservative with update for guiding principles

definitions.note: a credo is a single set of beliefs, here described by the plural principles it contains

parts.note: to update something is to redo it

explanation.surface: A Conservative party revising its guiding values.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a creed or statement of beliefs that steers someone's conduct.

clue.text: £25 should cover rising charges — thousand for Banksy, perhaps

indicators.note: the outer word is to wrap round the other piece

parts.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word charges' synonym reads upwards

parts.note: dues are charges or fees
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A query about how much a Banksy print costs: twenty-five pounds, or a thousand?
explanation.walkthrough: In British money slang a pony is £25; 'should cover' puts the upward-read charges inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Banksy is the assumed name of an anonymous street artist, an example of an alias.

clue.text: Delivering lad latest ASBO not a worry in the end

parts.note: the latest thing is new

indicators.note: not tells us to drop the next word's letter from ASBO

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word worry is used

parts.note: taken as written; its last letter is used

explanation.surface: A paperboy's newest behaviour order is nothing to worry about in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: An ASBO was a British Anti-Social Behaviour Order, imposed on troublesome youths. ASBO without A leaves SBO.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsboy is a boy who delivers or sells newspapers.

clue.text: Suspicion surrounding hotel in ancient region

indicators.note: the first word's synonym goes around the second's letter

parts.note: a trace or suspicion means a tiny hint
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A hint of doubt about some hotel in an old land.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrace was a historical territory in the south-east Balkans known to the Greeks and Romans.

clue.text: See 9
Mars socialist idea over case for employment

indicators.note: in a down clue the first pieces sit above the last one

parts.note: a red is a left-wing socialist
a plan is an idea or scheme

indicators.note: the case is the outer shell, the first and last letters of employment

parts.note: taken as written; only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: A left-wing idea about the case for jobs, hidden behind a brand of chocolate.
explanation.walkthrough: Mars looks like the chocolate bar or the war god; it is the planet nicknamed for its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The planet Mars is popularly known by this nickname because of its reddish iron-oxide surface.

clue.text: Orchestra, perhaps unloved, plays in cathedral city

indicators.note: plays means the remaining letters are rearranged as if performing
un-loved: love, the zero score, is taken away, so a round letter goes

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An orchestra, perhaps not much liked, performs in a French cathedral town.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is nil in tennis, hence O. ORCHESTRA less O gives RCHESTRA, which is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartres in France is famous for its Gothic cathedral and medieval stained glass.

clue.text: 14 recording dark matter image, and those needing adjustment

indicators.note: letters that need adjusting are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An astronomer's picture of dark matter, and the parts that still need correcting.
explanation.walkthrough: The 14 is Paul Simon (14-down), and this is the song title taking in 6-down and 13-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Take Me to the Mardi Gras is a 1973 song released by the singer-songwriter Paul Simon.

clue.text: Having contest no side wins, pull out

parts.note: with means having, as in a house with a garden
a draw is a game that neither side wins

explanation.surface: Having a contest that ends level, someone decides to quit.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw is to retreat or retire from something, the same as pulling out.

clue.text: Frenchman in Spanish city, expert swimmer

indicators.note: the Frenchman's letter is placed inside the city's name

parts.note: León is a city in northern Spain
M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, a Frenchman
a dab hand, or dab, is an expert

explanation.surface: A Frenchman living in a Spanish city turns out to be a champion swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dab' or 'dab hand' is British slang for an expert. 'Swimmer' looks like a description of the Frenchman but is the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The lemon dab is a flatfish of the North Atlantic, so the fish is a swimmer.

clue.text: Stone tool — it goes into collapsed hole

indicators.note: the small word is to be placed inside the other letters
a collapsed hole has its letters fallen into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction for a stone tool going into a hole that has caved in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapsed' looks like a description of the hole, but it signals that its letters are rearranged before the small word goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: An eolith is a crudely chipped flint once believed to be a very early human implement.

clue.text: Capital parking secured by villain in lucrative scheme

parts.note: capital means money

indicators.note: the villain's synonym holds the parking letter securely inside

parts.note: a sinner is a wrongdoer or villain
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: Money from parking fees held by a crook in a profitable racket.
explanation.definitionFit: A money-spinner is a business or idea that brings in plenty of profit.

clue.text: See 9
China has one day to allow entry for classy singer

indicators.note: the outer letters let the classy letter come in

parts.note: china plate is rhyming slang for mate, so a pal
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
has is shortened to 's, as in he's got
I is the Roman numeral one
MON is the abbreviation for Monday

explanation.surface: Fine porcelain gets one day's access for an upmarket vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate). 'Classy' gives U from the old British U and non-U class labels.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Simon is an American singer-songwriter, once of Simon and Garfunkel.

clue.text: Bizarre fatigue besetting million — what smoking can do

indicators.note: the rearranged letters surround the letter for million
bizarre means the letters are put into a strange new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange tiredness afflicting a million people, blamed on cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoking' suggests tobacco; here it is filling a space with smoke to disinfect it.
explanation.definitionFit: To fumigate is to disinfect a place with smoke or fumes, which smoking it out achieves.

clue.text: Criminal computer user appeal heard here

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters are corrupted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hacker's appeal against conviction will be heard in this court.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest court in the land hears final appeals on points of law.

clue.text: Players under guidance made double move in game

parts.note: the cast is the set of players in a show
being under guidance means being led

explanation.surface: Actors being directed in a play perform a two-part manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, castling moves king and rook together in a single turn.

clue.text: Gypsy Chorus sampled for Thriller

indicators.note: sampled says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of an operatic gypsy chorus used as a sample for a Michael Jackson album.
explanation.definitionFit: Psycho is the 1960 Hitchcock film, a classic example of a suspense movie.

clue.text: Learn by intuition and pass round the Bordeaux?

indicators.note: the word for pass goes around the wine word

parts.note: to pass away is to die
Bordeaux is a French wine, and the French for wine is vin

explanation.surface: Guessing by instinct and handing the claret round the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Bordeaux as an example: a French wine, hence the French word for wine.
explanation.definitionFit: To divine is to discover something by instinct or insight rather than reasoning.

clue.text: Keen listener gathering tips on grapevine

indicators.note: the listener's word gathers the other letters inside it

parts.note: an ear is a listener

indicators.note: the tips are the first and last letters of grapevine

parts.note: taken as written; only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: An eager eavesdropper picking up hints through the rumour network.
explanation.definitionFit: Being eager means being enthusiastic and keen to do something.

clue.text: Anticipation of wisdom keeping American quiet

indicators.note: the wisdom word keeps the other letters inside

parts.note: sense is good judgement or wisdom
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: Expecting wise words from a US citizen who keeps silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense is the anxious state of waiting for an outcome, i.e. tense expectation.

clue.text: MDMA with powder taken up brings striking effect

parts.note: MDMA is ecstasy, shortened to E

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up means the powder's word reads upwards

parts.note: talc is talcum powder

explanation.surface: Taking ecstasy alongside snorted powder gives a dramatic high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken up' hints at snorting; it turns TALC upwards to give CLAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat means conspicuous brilliance or dazzling success, a showy effect.

clue.text: Unbalanced cook with extremely antisocial air

parts.note: mentally unbalanced means mad
to cook the books is to rig them

indicators.note: the extremes are the first and last letters of antisocial

parts.note: taken as written; only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: A deranged chef with an extremely unfriendly manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' looks like a manner or demeanour; here it is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A madrigal is a part-song for several voices, and an air is a song or melody.

clue.text: Commons staff to hold one Liberal back for spite

indicators.note: the staff word holds the other letters inside

parts.note: the mace is the ceremonial staff of the House of Commons

indicators.note: back means the letters for one and Liberal are read in reverse

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Parliament's officials holding back a lone Liberal out of spite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commons staff' seems to mean employees; it is the Mace, the ceremonial club placed on the table in the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice is the desire to harm others, the same as spite.

clue.text: Domestic heater old man mentioned

indicators.note: mentioned means spoken, so the word is heard not read

parts.note: a geezer is British slang for an old man

explanation.surface: A domestic water heater that the old fellow referred to.
explanation.walkthrough: In British use a geyser is a gas water heater, and in British pronunciation it sounds like geezer, slang for a bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a geyser is a gas appliance that heats water for a house.

clue.text: Lecturer fighting to axe constant grant

parts.note: a don is a university lecturer

indicators.note: to axe something is to cut it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: action means fighting, as in killed in action
C is the constant for the speed of light

explanation.surface: An academic fighting to stop a permanent funding grant being cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant is a sum given, the same as a donation or gift.
